entities.name: Peter IV of Aragon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peter IV of Aragon, known as 'the Ceremonious' (el Ceremoniós or el del Punyalet), reigned as King of Aragon, Sardinia-Corsica, and Valencia, and Count of Barcelona from 1336 until his death on January 13, 1387. His 51-year rule was a pivotal period for the Crown of Aragon, characterized by an assertive expansion of royal power, the consolidation of Aragonese influence in the Mediterranean, and a complex interplay of dynastic ambition, constitutional negotiation, and military conflict across the Iberian Peninsula and beyond. He confronted internal challenges from the Aragonese and Valencian Unions, external threats from Castile, and solidified his realm's position as a major maritime power.

Peter IV's reign began with the decisive deposition of James III of Majorca in 1344, thereby annexing the Kingdom of Majorca and its associated Pyrenean counties (Roussillon, Cerdanya) directly into the Crown of Aragon, unifying the Aragonese and Majorcan branches of the House of Barcelona. He subsequently engaged in the long and costly War of the Two Peters (1356–1375) against Peter I of Castile, a conflict driven by territorial disputes over Murcia and dynastic rivalries that devastated parts of Aragon and Valencia. Domestically, he faced significant opposition from the Aragonese and Valencian Unions, noble and civic leagues demanding greater autonomy and constitutional rights, which he ultimately suppressed in 1348 at the Battle of Épila, strengthening royal authority. He also played a crucial, if pragmatic, role in the Western Schism, initially supporting the Avignon papacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Peter IV significantly consolidated royal power within the Crown of Aragon, unifying its various realms and laying the groundwork for its future Mediterranean expansion. His reign reshaped the political landscape of the eastern Iberian Peninsula, influencing subsequent Aragonese and Castilian relations.
